Learning Objectives
Evaluate the types of mutations and epigenetic changes that cause disease.
Identify the manner in which mutations that encode for proteins with various function cause
disease.
Compare clinical similarities of conditions caused by genes with protein products that have
similar functions.
Review a classification system to keep categorize genetic diseases of the musculoskeletal
system .


Causes of Genetic Diseases
Genetic diseases are caused by a permanent change in DNA in the cells in the body.
Genetic changes can be germ line, affecting all the cells in the body, such as in patients
with neurofibromatosis, or somatic, affecting only some cells, such as in patients with
polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. Such a change can be an inherited mutation or result from
a chance error during cell replication. Mutations range from one nucleic acid change
causing a functional change in a single protein to a large chromosomal abnormality
involving thousands of genes. Disease also may be caused by environmental factors that
change the expression of multiple genes. Teratogens and carcinogens cause disease in
this manner; fetal alcohol syndrome is an example.1
Some environmental influences have epigenetic effects, which are heritable phenotype
changes that do not involve alterations in the DNA sequence but instead are caused by
changes in proteins strongly associated with DNA. Conditions such as Beckwith-
Wiedemann syndrome are inherited this manner, and many cancers are driven by
epigenetic changes.2
Some disorders also may result from a combination of genetic and environmental
effects, such as some types of congenital scoliosis in which a heterozygous mutation that
typically does not cause disease produces a hemivertebra if a fetus is exposed to anoxia
at certain times during development.3
Genetic diseases also can be caused by mutations that change DNA confirmation, such
as alternating topologic chromatin domains. By altering confirmation without causing a
change in any specific gene, the expression of multiple genes is altered, causing disease
such as congenital limb deformity.4,5
Identifying a DNA change does not mean a mutation that causes a disease has been
found because many DNA changes are part of normal variability. The criteria for calling a
mutation causative recently have been established by a consensus panel.6

Therefore, whole genome sequencing alone may not be effective in diagnosis.7,8
As technology advances and knowledge of genetics improves, such technologies will
likely become mainstream in clinical settings.9
The broad spectrum of genetic diseases of musculoskeletal tissue results in difficultly
understand them. In addition, the rapid pace of molecular genetic research is reshaping
the manner in which physicians think about these syndromes. The traditional
nomenclature for these disorders occasionally is confounded by the different diseases
caused by mutations in the same gene.
Grouping diseases according to the function of the causative gene mutation is useful.
Such a classification scheme may aid in diagnosis, management, or understanding the
pathophysiology of disease because genetic disorders caused by similar types of genes
often share clinical similarities. For example, disorders caused by mutations regulating
growth of tissues result in the potential for malignancy. Although grouping these
disorders into broad categories based on the type of underlying causative gene will not
be all-inclusive, such classification is straightforward method and clinically useful.10,11
Details regarding specific disorders can be found on the GeneReviews website (Resource
1).
Structural Genes
The gene defect causing these disorders results in an abnormality in a protein important for
maintaining the structural properties of the musculoskeletal system.
The type of structural gene involved and the tissue in which it is expressed predicts the
manner in which the disease behaves. The defective protein product causes a mechanical
defect in involved tissues.
The phenotype can evolve with time because the abnormal structural components of the
connective tissues slowly fail or wear out as the individual grows. These disorders usually are
inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.
Cell function generally is normal in patients with these conditions, and no predisposition to
malignancy exists.
Deformity often recurs postoperatively because the structural components are abnormal and
will wear out again.

If the structural abnormality involves cartilage, growth abnormality caused by physeal
mechanical failure or early degenerative joint disease caused by articular cartilage failure may
occur. If a protein important in ligament strength is affected, joints often subluxate.
In many of these disorders, heterogeneity is present in the clinical manifestations, depending
on how much of and in what manner the structural protein is abnormal. For example, in
patients with osteogenesis imperfecta, which is caused by a mutation regulating type I collagen
(the major type of collagen in bone), mild or severe clinical findings may be present depending
on the actual type of mutation.
In patients with mild disease, life expectancy is normal; however, in patients with more severe
disease, life expectancy may be shortened because of secondary effects of the structural
defects on vital organs.
Osteogenesis imperfecta involves type I collagen, which is expressed in bone, skin, eyes, and
various other tissues. Therefore, a mechanical defect is present in the bones, but the bones
are patterned normally. In many subtypes, the sclera is blue because of the abnormal collagen
in the eye (Resource 2).

Structural Genes
Marfan syndrome involves the fibrillin gene. This protein product helps maintain the
elastic properties of the soft connective tissues. These tissues are lax and may result in
joint subluxation. The blood vessel walls also are affected, resulting in dilatations of
cardiovascular structures. The characteristic tall stature, long fingers, and long toes that
are characteristic of Marfan syndrome are the result of abnormal fibrillin binding to
growth factors, releasing them at greater than normal levels with growth (Resource 3).
Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia involves type II collagen. Because this collagen type is
primarily expressed by chondrocytes, the cartilage is affected, resulting in short bones
because of early chondroepiphyseal problems or later growth plate problems.
Degenerative joint disease is common because the articular cartilage matrix cannot
withstand the forces it is subjected to with normal activity (Resource 4).
Tumor-Related Genes

The abnormality in these genes results in a dysfunction in the normal cell cycle control,
resulting in increased cell growth or a defect in normal cell differentiation.
These diseases usually are caused by a mutation in one copy of the gene and are inherited in
an autosomal dominant manner.
In most patients, the clinical manifestation is overgrowth of a specific tissue type. If the other
copy of the defective gene is lost or mutated in a somatic manner, a more aggressive tumor
can develop.
The risk of malignant progression can result in a shortened life span.
Overgrowth, or recurrence, often occurs postoperatively because the underlying genetic
defect is not corrected by the surgical procedure.

Tumor-Related Genes
Neurofibromatosis type I and multiple enchondromatosis are examples of disorders that
fall into this category. The mutation in neurofibromatosis type I is germ line in the NF1
gene; the protein product of this gene regulates activation of the Ras signaling pathway.
Activation of the signaling pathway leads to the development of neurofibromas,
pseudarthrosis, and growth abnormality. If the normal allele of the NF1 gene is lost,
more invasive tumors may arise (Resource 5).
Multiple enchondromatosis may be caused by somatic mutations in one of the isocitrate
dehydrogenase genes. The protein products of these genes regulate the tricarboxylic
acid cycle (or Krebs cycle), and mutations in chondrocytes block differentiation, resulting
in the persistence of growth plate chondrocytes after skeletal maturity. The benign
tumors in these patients may progress to chondrosarcoma.12
Developmental Patterning Genes
During embryonic development, cell signaling systems are activated in a coordinated manner
to cause cells to proliferate, move, and undergo programmed cell death to allow the organism
to normally pattern and develop into an adult. Mutations in genes that encode proteins that
play roles in these pathways alter normal patterning, resulting in a malformation.

Disorders caused by mutations in such genes often can be identified at birth because the
problem is present at the beginning of development; however, the phenotype may not be
obvious until the child is older.
Because these are patterning problems, surgery to correct malalignment may be successful.
Manifestations in other organ systems are frequent because the same developmental
signaling pathways play a key role in the development of multiple organs.
Symptoms from the malformations often increase with age because the abnormally shaped
structures cannot sustain the stresses of normal activity. These disorders usually are inherited
in an autosomal dominant manner.

Developmental Patterning Genes
Achondroplasia is caused by a mutation in the FGFR3 gene. Fibroblast growth factor
regulates chondrocytes early in development, and the mutation interferes with the
normal progression of chondrocyte maturation. The entire chondroepiphysis develops
abnormally, with greater effect in regions of greatest endochondral growth, giving rise to
the characteristic rhizomelic shortening (ie, more shortening of the proximal bones). A
congenital spinal stenosis is associated with a narrow space between the pedicles in the
lumbar spine because of greater than normal growth of the larger bones (Resource 6).
Protein Processing Genes (Enzymes)
These genes often modify substances for degradation or encode proteins that process other
proteins, altering their function (eg, by adding sulfate groups). Mutations in genes in this
category may have various effects on cells, resulting in a wide range of clinical findings.
Many of these disorders result in the excess accumulation of proteins in cells. In such patients,
the cells become larger than normal, resulting in increased pressure in bones and causing an
osteonecrosis-like phenotype and increased extradural material in the spine.
Medical treatment options to replace the defective enzyme have been developed for many of
these disorders; however, such management often will arrest but not reverse the skeletal
manifestations of the disorder.
Most enzyme disorders are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.


Protein Processing Genes (Enzymes)
The mucopolysaccharidoses are a class of disorders caused by mutations in protein
processing genes. Mucopolysaccharidoses are caused by abnormal functioning of
lysosomal enzymes that degrades sulfonated glycosaminoglycans. The incomplete
degradation product accumulates in the lysosomes. Various subtypes, classified by the
specific enzyme involved, exist. Features common to these disorders include corneal
clouding, organomegaly, epiphyseal deformation, contractures, cardiac disease, and
deafness. Hurler syndrome is the most common type and is severe, with patients living
only to their teenage years unless treated for the enzyme deficiency. Hunter syndrome is
less severe, with patients having a normal life span. Children with Hunter syndrome have
upper cervical instability, kyphosis of any region of the spine, hip deformity, and
malalignment of the lower limbs (Resource 7).
Genes Important in Nerve or Muscle Function
Neurologic disorders can be caused by mutations in genes that encode for proteins that
regulate neuron function, muscle function, or peripheral nerve conduction.
These diseases cause bone and joint anomalies and occur secondary to abnormal nerve or
muscle function.
Osteopenia often occurs secondary to abnormal muscle tone.
The course of these disorders is variable; however, several are associated with progressive
weakness.
Various inheritance patterns exist; however, many of these disorders are linked to the X
chromosome. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner, and
Rett syndrome is inherited in an X-linked dominant manner.
Some disorders in this group are caused by mitochondrial genes, which are only of maternal
origin.
Disorders involving the muscles or the central nervous system are associated with a shortened
life span, whereas disorders involving the peripheral nervous system usually are compatible
with a normal life span.
Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, spinal muscular atrophy, and
Rett syndrome are examples of disorders in this category.

Chromosome Abnormalities (Multiple Genes)
Chromosomal abnormalities involve substantial portions of DNA, and multiple genes often are
affected. Deletions, duplications, or translocations can occur. Somatic changes can cause
neoplasia. Large abnormalities in chromosomes almost always are associated with some
degree of mental deficiency.
Because multiple genes are abnormal in all cells, cell functions (such as the ability to mount an
immune response or normal wound healing) also may be abnormal.
With the exception of rare instances, these disorders are not inherited and occur as sporadic
events. Down syndrome and Turner syndrome are chromosomal disorders for which patients
often are referred to orthopaedic surgeons.

Chromosome Abnormalities (Multiple Genes)
Down syndrome is caused by trisomy 21. Patients have characteristic facies, with upward
slanting eyes, epicanthal folds, and a flattened profile. The hands display one transverse
flexion crease, often called a simian crease. Affected individuals have a short stature.
Although intellectual disability is present, wide variation exists in the intelligent quotient,
and children often fare better than expected. Congenital heart disease, duodenal atresia,
and auditory loss can occur. Approximately 1% of patients with Down syndrome develop
leukemia. A high incidence of endocrinopathy, particularly hypothyroidism, is reported.
Infections are common; however, the reason for this is unclear. One of five individuals
with Down syndrome has a musculoskeletal problem related primarily to joint instability.
Although this instability is attributed to ligamentous laxity, other factors, such as
changes in the shape of the joints and changes in the site of ligament insertions, also
may contribute. The outcome of surgical management for joint instability in individuals
with Down syndrome is not as good as that in individuals without Down syndrome,
which likely is related to multiple factors, including abnormal cell behavior attributable to
trisomy 21, abnormal joint shapes, and laxity of the soft tissues. In 10% of patients, an
increased atlantoaxial distance is observed on radiographs of the cervical spine;
however, treatment of these patients is controversial.13
Turner syndrome is caused by one X chromosome and occurs only in girls. Affected girls
have a webbed neck, low hairline, short stature, and sexual infantilism. Because of a lack

of sex steroid hormones, puberty does not occur and secondary sex characteristics do
not develop. Currently, most children are treated with exogenous estrogen. Growth
hormone also has been administered, resulting in a height increase of approximately 8
cm; however, growth hormone supplementation remains controversial. Scoliosis and
varus deformity of the elbow are common. Most individuals have low bone density,
which is thought to be related to the lack of sex steroid hormone.
Girls with only one X chromosome are susceptible to X-linked recessive disorders, such
as Duchenne muscular dystrophy14 (Table 1).
